title: “I AM DOING A NEW THING” — BUT WHAT IF THE FIRST THING GOD WANTS TO CHANGE IS YOU?
paragraphs: “I AM DOING A NEW THING” — BUT WHAT IF THE FIRST THING GOD WANTS TO CHANGE IS YOU?

Isaiah 43:19 was never simply a promise of a new job, a new relationship, or a better opportunity. It was spoken to people who had lost almost everything—and it reveals something far greater than the fresh start we keep asking God to give us.
There is something heartbreaking about a person who keeps asking God for a new beginning while secretly refusing to let Him touch the very thing that is destroying their life.
They want a new relationship, but they keep carrying the same unhealed bitterness.
They want a new job, but their identity still rises and falls with their paycheck.
They want a new season, but they are still negotiating with the sin that devastated the last one.
They want God to open another door.
But what if God is calling them to stop running through doors that lead them away from Him?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable possibility of all...
What if you have been praying for God to change your circumstances while He has been patiently calling you to surrender your heart?
Before you claim Isaiah 43:19 as your personal announcement of promotion, marriage, financial breakthrough, or sudden opportunity, you need to hear what God was actually saying.
Because this verse is more beautiful than the motivational captions we have built around it.
And far more confronting.
“Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.” — Isaiah 43:19 (KJV)
Beautiful, isn't it?
But do you know who first heard those words?
Not someone waiting for a promotion.
Not a single person hoping to meet the love of their life.
Not an entrepreneur waiting for a business breakthrough.
God was speaking to His covenant people, Israel, in a prophetic message of restoration from exile.
A people whose national life had been shattered.
A people facing the bitter consequences of rebellion, judgment, displacement, and loss.
A people who needed more than improved circumstances.
They needed the God they had repeatedly turned away from.
And this is where the verse begins to cut deeper than most people expect.
Because God was not simply promising to make their lives more comfortable.
He was announcing that their failure would not have the final word over His redemptive purposes.
Read that again.
Their failure would not have the final word over God's redemptive purposes.
That is the kind of new beginning Scripture is talking about.
And if you have ever looked at your life and wondered whether you have ruined too much to be restored, this message is for you.
Isaiah 43 does not begin with God pretending Israel had been faithful.
He knew their history.
He knew their idolatry.
He knew their disobedience.
He knew how often they had exchanged His glory for things that could never save them.
Yet listen to what He says earlier in the chapter:
“But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.” — Isaiah 43:1 (KJV)
Thou art mine.
Imagine hearing those words when everything around you seems to testify that your story is finished.
When the consequences of yesterday are still sitting beside you at breakfast.
When people remember the version of you that you desperately wish they would forget.
When you have apologized, repented, cried, tried to rebuild, and still cannot escape the memory of what happened.
When you wonder whether God sees anything in you beyond your worst decision.
And then, through His Word, you encounter the God who redeems.
Not a God who calls evil good.
Not a God who dismisses rebellion as harmless.
But the holy God who is able to restore people who could never rescue themselves.
That is the heart of this passage.
To understand it properly, we need to look at the words God actually inspired through the prophet Isaiah.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 43:19 begins:
הִנְנִי עֹשֶׂה חֲדָשָׁה
Hinnēnī ʿōśeh ḥădāšāh.
A faithful rendering is:
“Behold, I am doing a new thing.”
The word ḥădāšāh (חֲדָשָׁה) means something new.
The expression emphasizes God's own action.
Notice who is doing the work.
Not Israel.
Not the strength of their determination.
Not their ability to manufacture a breakthrough.
God Himself.
And that matters because the people receiving this promise were not being told to create their own salvation.
They were being called to recognize the saving action of the Lord.
The next words are equally powerful:
עַתָּה תִצְמָח
ʿAttāh tiṣmāḥ.
“Now it shall spring forth.”
The verb tiṣmāḥ comes from a Hebrew root associated with sprouting or growing.
It evokes the picture of something emerging into view.
Something God is bringing forth.
Something that may not yet be fully visible to those who desperately need it.
But do not turn that beautiful image into a guarantee that every private ambition is about to succeed.
The passage is not saying that every desire you have is a seed God has promised to grow.
It is saying that God is able to accomplish His saving purposes where human beings see no way forward.
And the historical context makes this extraordinary.
Earlier in the passage, Isaiah recalls the Lord who made a path through the sea, drawing attention to Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Isaiah 43:16–17).
Then God announces:
“Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old.” — Isaiah 43:18 (KJV)
Does that mean God's people were commanded to erase their memories?
Of course not.
Throughout Scripture, Israel was repeatedly instructed to remember God's mighty acts.
The point is not spiritual amnesia.
The point is that Israel must not imagine God's future deliverance is limited to the exact pattern of His past deliverance.
The God who once made a path through the sea could now make a path through the wilderness.
The God who once delivered His people from Egypt could bring His exiled people home.
God was not trapped in yesterday's miracle.
And neither should His people assume that yesterday's experience exhausted what He could do.
That is the original beauty of Isaiah 43:19.
The Lord was promising a new act of deliverance, not distributing blank checks for every dream His people might have.
And that distinction may save someone from years of unnecessary disappointment.
Because perhaps you have been told that if you believe hard enough, God must give you the relationship.
If you declare Isaiah 43:19 often enough, the money must arrive.
If you post the verse, claim the verse, repeat the verse, and refuse to entertain doubt, the opportunity must come.
But what happens when the opportunity does not come?
What happens when the person you prayed would stay decides to leave?
What happens when the business closes?
When the test results are not what you hoped?
When you lose the job instead of receiving the promotion?
When you are still waiting after everyone else seems to have moved forward?
Does that mean God has failed?
Does that mean you did not have enough faith?
No.
It means Isaiah 43:19 was never a divine obligation to fulfill every earthly expectation.
God's faithfulness is not measured by how closely His decisions resemble your plans.
Sometimes His providence includes a door opening.
Sometimes it includes a door closing.
Sometimes His kindness is experienced through unexpected provision.
Sometimes His sustaining grace carries us through suffering that does not immediately disappear.
And sometimes the deepest work God is doing cannot be photographed, announced, or celebrated in a social media testimony.
Because nobody can see repentance happening inside a heart.
Nobody can measure the moment pride finally begins to surrender.
Nobody knows how much courage it takes for someone to delete a secret conversation, confess a hidden sin, ask forgiveness, or choose obedience when nobody is watching.
But heaven is not indifferent to what happens in secret.
Jesus taught that the Father sees what is done in secret (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18).
And perhaps the new thing you need most is not something the world will applaud.
Perhaps it is the grace to become truthful again.
Perhaps it is the strength to forgive.
Perhaps it is the humility to admit you were wrong.
Perhaps it is the willingness to stop calling something a blessing when it keeps leading you into disobedience.
Perhaps it is learning that your value was never determined by whether somebody chose to stay.
Perhaps it is discovering that Jesus is enough even when the answer you wanted never comes.
That does not mean every painful experience is a punishment from God.
Scripture refuses that simplistic conclusion.
In John 9:1–3, Jesus challenged the assumption that a man's blindness must have resulted from a particular personal or parental sin.
Not every wilderness is the consequence of rebellion.
Some suffering comes because we live in a fallen world.
Some comes through the wrongdoing of others.
Some accompanies faithful obedience.
And sometimes we simply do not know why a particular sorrow has entered our lives.
But whatever the cause, the wilderness does not place us beyond the reach of God's mercy.
That is one of the most astonishing truths running through Isaiah.
The Lord does not abandon His redemptive purposes because His people are powerless.
He acts.
He rescues.
He restores.
And as the book of Isaiah unfolds, the promise of restoration points beyond the immediate return from exile toward the greater saving work God will accomplish through His Servant.
Isaiah 53 presents the suffering Servant who bears the sins of many.
The New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of this suffering and saving mission (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:24).
And now we begin to see the deeper beauty of the story.
Because the greatest new thing God has accomplished is not merely the restoration of earthly circumstances.
It is the redemption He has brought through Jesus Christ.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed sinners without celebrating their sin.
He exposed hypocrisy without abandoning compassion.
He called people to repentance while offering mercy to those who knew they needed it.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because human beings had finally become worthy.
But because sinners needed a Savior.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8 (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully repaired our reputation.
Not after we had proven that we would never fail again.
Not after we had cleaned up every part of our history.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's grace truly is.
The cross tells us that forgiveness is not cheap.
And the resurrection tells us that sin and death do not have the final victory.
This is where the message becomes painfully personal.
Because you can get a new job and still be enslaved to greed.
You can enter a new relationship and still be ruled by jealousy.
You can move to a new city and carry the same secret addictions.
You can build a new public image while remaining spiritually exhausted behind closed doors.
You can even become more active in church while quietly drifting away from genuine intimacy with Christ.
A new environment does not automatically create a new heart.
A new opportunity does not erase guilt.
A new relationship cannot accomplish what only reconciliation with God can accomplish.
And that is why the New Testament gives us a declaration far greater than any motivational slogan:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
The original Greek begins:
ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις
Hōste ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ—a new creation.”
The expression kainē ktisis means “new creation.”
This is not merely the idea of rearranging an old life until it looks more attractive.
Paul is speaking about the reality of belonging to Christ and participating in the new-creation work God has begun through Him.
Notice the condition.
In Christ.
Not merely inspired by Christ.
Not merely familiar with Christian language.
Not merely someone who shares Bible verses when life becomes difficult.
In Christ.
United to Him by faith.
Reconciled to God through Him.
Called into a life shaped by His grace and lordship.
And that changes the entire conversation about new beginnings.
Because the greatest question is no longer, “God, when will You give me something new?”
It becomes, “Lord Jesus, am I truly Yours?”
That question may be uncomfortable.
But it is far too important to avoid.
You can know every popular promise about breakthrough and still fail to understand the Gospel.
You can be excited about God's blessings while remaining resistant to His commands.
You can want the benefits of Christianity without wanting the Christ who calls you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him (Luke 9:23).
And there is a tragedy in wanting Jesus to transform everything around you while refusing to surrender anything within you.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8?
Her shame had become public.
Her accusers wanted condemnation.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of those who stood ready to stone her.
And when her accusers had departed, He told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Compassion.
And a summons to a different life.
Jesus did not tell her that her sin was beautiful.
He did not say that repentance was unnecessary.
He did not reduce her entire identity to her worst moment either.
He offered mercy while calling her away from sin.
That is the grace we desperately need.
Not a counterfeit grace that leaves us comfortable in destruction.
Not a crushing religion that convinces us our past makes redemption impossible.
But the grace of Jesus Christ that forgives, restores, and transforms.
And perhaps that is what you have been missing.
You thought you needed another chance to prove yourself.
But what you truly needed was to come to the Savior who already knows everything about you.
The things you admit.
The things you hide.
The things you regret.
The things you still defend.
The moments you wish you could relive.
The words you cannot take back.
The people you hurt.
The wounds others left in you.
The compromises you once promised you would never make.
He knows.
And still, the Gospel announces that everyone who turns to Christ in repentance and faith may receive forgiveness and new life.
Not because their sin was harmless.
But because His sacrifice is sufficient.
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.” — Ephesians 1:7 (KJV)
Think about that.
Your history may contain a scandal.
Your conscience may carry regret.
Your reputation may have suffered.
Your consequences may still be real.
And not every broken earthly relationship will necessarily be restored.
But your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Because Jesus Christ is able to save.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not that Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not that consequences disappear automatically.
Not that every person we hurt must immediately trust us again.
But that our sin does not have to remain our identity, our condemnation does not have to remain our destiny, and our brokenness does not have to be the end of our story.
In Christ, forgiveness is real.
Repentance matters.
Restoration is possible.
And transformation begins with the grace of God, not with the performance of a perfect person.
Maybe you are reading this while waiting for something.
A job offer.
A medical answer.
A reconciliation.
A financial breakthrough.
A husband.
A wife.
A child.
A chance to rebuild after a humiliating failure.
There is nothing wrong with bringing those desires before the Lord.
Scripture invites believers to pray about their needs (Philippians 4:6–7).
Ask Him.
Trust Him.
Seek His wisdom.
But do not reduce His goodness to the outcome you prefer.
And do not mistake a delayed answer for an absent Savior.
The same Jesus who conquered the grave is worthy of your trust when the road ahead remains unclear.
You may not receive every new thing you desire.
But everyone who belongs to Christ has something infinitely greater than a guarantee of earthly success.
They have a living Savior.
They have forgiveness.
They have the Holy Spirit.
They have the promise that God will complete the good work He has begun in them (Philippians 1:6).
And they have a future resurrection hope that no disappointment in this present age can destroy.
One day, the new creation will be fully revealed.
Revelation 21:5 records the words of the One seated upon the throne:
“Behold, I make all things new.”
Not merely a new opportunity.
Not merely a better season.
Not merely a temporary escape from pain.
All things new.
A new heaven and a new earth.
The end of death, mourning, crying, and pain.
The full and final triumph of God's redemptive purposes through Jesus Christ.
That is where the Christian hope is ultimately headed.
And suddenly Isaiah 43:19 becomes more than a verse to post when life is going well.
It becomes a testimony to the character of the God who saves.
The God who makes a way where His people cannot make one.
The God whose faithfulness outlasts human failure.
The God whose promises find their ultimate “Yes” in Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).
So when you read, “I am doing a new thing,” do not rush past the One who is speaking.
Do not become so fascinated with the gift that you overlook the Giver.
Do not become so consumed with your next season that you neglect your eternal soul.
And please...
Do not spend your whole life asking God to change your story while resisting the Savior who came to redeem it.
Maybe the most important prayer you can offer today is not, “Lord, give me something new.”
Maybe it is this:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent so much time asking You to change what is happening around me that I have neglected what needs to change within me. Forgive my sins. Expose what I have hidden. Heal what is wounded. Teach me to repent where I have rebelled. Give me the courage to obey even when obedience costs me something. Help me trust Your wisdom when Your answer is different from my desires. I do not merely want a better life. I need You. Make me more like You. Amen.”
And if that prayer expresses what is happening in your heart, do not rush away from this moment.
You do not have to pretend that you have everything figured out.
You do not have to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
You can simply be truthful.
You do not need to reveal private details. Even a few honest words can open the door for another believer to encourage you in prayer.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that repentance, forgiveness, and a changed life are not merely religious ideas.
They are realities of God's grace.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message.
Someone who has been interpreting every closed door as proof that God has abandoned them.
Someone who believes their past disqualifies them from ever coming home to Christ.
Someone who has been chasing one breakthrough after another while their soul is starving for the Gospel.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because an algorithm determines spiritual faithfulness.
But because the truth of Jesus Christ deserves to be made known, and a simple act of sharing may place biblical encouragement before someone who would never have searched for it.
Because faith was never meant to survive on occasional inspiration alone.
We need the Word of God.
We need prayer.
We need the fellowship and accountability of the local church.
We need faithful teaching that points us back to Jesus when our emotions are pulling us in a hundred different directions.
And that is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the church.
Not to sell God's blessings.
Not to turn the Gospel into a transaction.
But to help make Christ-centered biblical encouragement and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
These resources are offered freely because we believe biblical nourishment should not be reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
But keeping resources accessible, creating thoughtful biblical content, and reaching more people requires ongoing support.
For Christians who are able to give, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a genuine expression of generosity and worship.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly, or of necessity.
Biblical giving is not supposed to be extracted through fear, guilt, or emotional pressure.
It does not guarantee a financial breakthrough.
And it is not a substitute for the giving, stewardship, and responsibilities you prayerfully practice through your local church.
It can be part of how you steward what God has entrusted to you for the benefit of others.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The resources, the articles, the books, the community, and the ongoing work are meant to serve something greater: helping people encounter biblical truth and grow as disciples of Christ.
You are still welcome.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Pointing even one person toward the truth of Jesus Christ is worthwhile.
Because the goal is not to build a community impressed by our name.
The goal is to help people know His Name.
And before you leave, return with me to that opening question.
What if the first thing God wants to change is you?
Not because every problem in your life is your fault.
Not because God is withholding His love until you improve yourself.
But because the greatest gift He can give you is not an easier life separated from Him.
It is reconciliation with Himself through Jesus Christ.
The God who promised a way through the wilderness has revealed the fullness of His saving grace in the Savior who declared:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6 (KJV)
There it is.
The answer beneath all our searching.
The hope beyond every closed door.
The Savior greater than every new opportunity.
You may still be waiting for the job.
You may still be grieving the relationship.
You may still be rebuilding after the scandal.
You may still be walking through a wilderness with questions you cannot answer.
But the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Repent and believe.
Receive the forgiveness only He can give.
Follow Him, even when the path is difficult.
And remember that the God who began His saving work will not fail to accomplish His eternal purposes.
Because sometimes the miracle is not that God gives you the life you once imagined.
Sometimes the miracle is that, through Jesus Christ, He gives you a new life you could never have created for yourself.
You were begging God for a new chapter, while Jesus was offering you something far greater—a new creation.
